name: Rheumatoid Arthritis
summary: A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints, causing pain, swelling, and — if untreated — lasting joint damage.
symptoms: stiff hands that loosen up during the day
joint pain on both sides of the body
fatigue that doesn't go away with rest
small lumps under the skin near joints

overview.whatIsIt: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system, which normally protects the body from infection, mistakenly targets the thin lining (synovium) that surrounds the joints. That misdirected attack causes inflammation, which leads to pain, swelling, warmth, and stiffness — usually starting in the small joints of the hands and feet and often affecting the same joints on both sides of the body. Over time, unchecked inflammation can erode cartilage and bone, changing the shape of joints and limiting how they move. Nobody fully knows why the immune system turns on the joints this way, but genetics, smoking, certain infections, and other environmental factors all appear to play a role. RA is not something you caused by anything you did or didn't do, and it is not contagious — you cannot catch it from, or pass it to, another person.
keyPoints: RA affects an estimated 1.3 million adults in the United States, roughly 0.6% to 1% of the population, and can start at any age but most often appears between the ages of 30 and 60.
It is two to three times more common in women than men, and about three out of four people living with RA are women.
It's driven by the immune system attacking the joint lining rather than by wear-and-tear, infection, or lifestyle choices; genetics and smoking are among the best-established risk factors.

Typical early signs are symmetric joint pain and stiffness — especially in the morning — along with fatigue and sometimes low-grade fever; the course varies from mild and intermittent to steadily progressive.

Left inadequately treated, RA can lead to permanent joint damage, disability, and a higher risk of cardiovascular disease; with early, sustained treatment, many people reach low disease activity or remission and avoid major joint damage.

Treatment has changed substantially since the 1990s: biologic drugs (introduced starting in the late 1990s) and JAK-inhibitor pills (approved starting in 2012) now let many people control RA far more effectively than older regimens alone, and current guidelines emphasize treating early and adjusting quickly if a first drug doesn't work well enough.

research.title: 2010 Rheumatoid arthritis classification criteria: an American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism collaborative initiative
research.authors: Aletaha D, Neogi T, Silman AJ, Funovits J, Felson DT, Bingham CO 3rd, et al.
research.summary: This is the paper that created the classification system rheumatologists still use to identify RA today. Because the older 1987 criteria were built to spot advanced, longstanding disease, this joint ACR/EULAR effort designed a scoring system — based on which and how many joints are involved, blood test results, inflammation markers, and how long symptoms have lasted — that can flag RA much earlier, when treatment has the best chance of preventing joint damage.

research.title: Rheumatoid arthritis
research.authors: Smolen JS, Aletaha D, McInnes IB
research.summary: A widely cited, comprehensive review of what's known about RA — how it develops, how it's diagnosed, and how it's treated. It lays out the case for the 'treat-to-target' approach that now underlies most rheumatology care: setting a specific disease-activity goal, checking progress regularly, and switching or adding medications promptly if that goal isn't being met, rather than waiting to see how things go.

research.title: Biologics or tofacitinib for people with rheumatoid arthritis naive to methotrexate: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
research.authors: Singh JA, Hossain A, Mudano AS, Tanjong Ghogomu E, Suarez-Almazor ME, Buchbinder R, Maxwell LJ, Tugwell P, Wells GA
research.summary: A Cochrane systematic review pooling 19 clinical trials (nearly 6,500 people) comparing biologic drugs plus methotrexate against methotrexate alone in people newly starting treatment. It found that adding a biologic gave a statistically significant, clinically meaningful boost to symptom control and the chance of remission, without a meaningful increase in serious side effects in these trials — though the reviewers noted more long-term safety data was still needed, especially for tofacitinib.

research.title: EULAR recommendations for the management of rheumatoid arthritis with synthetic and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs: 2025 update
research.authors: Smolen JS, Edwards CJ, Konzett V, Laskou F, Aletaha D, Caporali R, et al.
research.summary: The newest update to Europe's leading RA treatment guideline, streamlined to five overarching principles and nine recommendations. It keeps methotrexate (often with short-term steroids) as the starting point, but supports moving to a biologic sooner if that isn't working within 3 to 6 months, gives more specific guidance on weighing heart-disease, cancer, and blood-clot risk before starting a JAK inhibitor, and notes that falling biosimilar prices have made biologic therapy more accessible.

lifestyle.title: Diet & nutrition
lifestyle.guidance: There's no single required 'RA diet,' but the Arthritis Foundation points to an anti-inflammatory eating pattern similar to the Mediterranean diet — rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish, and olive oil, and lighter on red meat, refined sugar, and highly processed foods — as helpful for many people alongside medical treatment. Maintaining a weight that's healthy for you also matters, since extra weight places more mechanical stress on joints and is linked with higher inflammation. Fish oil (omega-3) supplements have some supporting evidence for easing joint tenderness, but talk with your rheumatologist before starting any supplement, since some can interact with RA medications.

lifestyle.title: Physical activity
lifestyle.guidance: It can feel counterintuitive, but the Arthritis Foundation and American College of Rheumatology both recommend staying active rather than resting joints — regular, moderate exercise (aiming toward about 150 minutes a week of activities like walking, swimming, or cycling) helps preserve joint function, muscle strength, and mood, and doesn't accelerate joint damage in RA. Low-impact options and range-of-motion exercises are especially useful during flares, and a physical or occupational therapist can help build a plan suited to which joints are affected. Start gradually and adjust intensity around flares rather than pushing through significant pain.

lifestyle.title: Emotional wellbeing
lifestyle.guidance: Living with a chronic, unpredictable disease takes a real emotional toll — the Arthritis Foundation notes that depression and anxiety are notably more common among people with RA than in the general population, partly because of the disease's inflammatory effects on the brain and partly because of the stress of managing a lifelong condition. Support groups (in person or through the Arthritis Foundation's online communities), counseling, and simple daily habits like pacing activity and prioritizing sleep all help. Mention mood or energy changes to your care team — they're a legitimate part of managing RA, not something to push through alone.

treatments.name: Methotrexate
treatments.description: A conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (csDMARD) and the standard first-choice medication for most newly diagnosed RA, per current ACR guidelines. Taken weekly as a pill or injection, it works by broadly calming an overactive immune response and, for many people, is combined with other DMARDs if it doesn't control disease on its own.

treatments.name: Biologic DMARDs (e.g., TNF inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, abatacept, rituximab)
treatments.description: Lab-engineered drugs, usually given by injection or infusion, that block specific parts of the immune system driving joint inflammation. Guidelines recommend adding a biologic when methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs aren't enough; several classes exist, so if one doesn't work well, switching to a different mechanism is a normal next step rather than a sign of treatment failure.

treatments.name: JAK inhibitors (e.g., tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib)
treatments.description: Oral targeted synthetic DMARDs that block signaling pathways (Janus kinases) inside immune cells. They're an alternative to biologics when methotrexate isn't sufficient, though the latest EULAR guidance recommends caution and closer risk discussion in people with cardiovascular disease, blood clot risk, cancer history, or who are over 65, based on accumulating safety data.

treatments.name: Short-term glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone)
treatments.description: Steroid medications that quickly reduce inflammation and are often used as a 'bridge' while a DMARD takes effect (which can take weeks), or for flare control. Because long-term use carries risks (including bone loss, weight gain, and elevated blood sugar), current guidelines recommend using the lowest effective dose for the shortest time possible.

treatments.name: Physical & occupational therapy
treatments.description: Therapists help preserve joint range of motion, build supporting muscle strength, and recommend joint-protection techniques or assistive devices for daily tasks. This is typically used alongside medication, not instead of it, and is especially useful when specific joints are affected or after a flare.

treatments.name: Rheumatoid factor & anti-CCP antibody testing
treatments.description: Blood tests that look for antibodies associated with RA and help confirm the diagnosis; a positive anti-CCP result is fairly specific to RA and can also help predict a more aggressive disease course, which factors into treatment decisions.

treatments.name: Routine disease-activity monitoring (labs, joint exams, imaging)
treatments.description: Regular visits combine a joint exam, inflammation markers (ESR, CRP), and sometimes X-rays or ultrasound to track disease activity using a standardized score. This 'treat-to-target' monitoring is how a rheumatologist decides whether the current treatment is working well enough or needs to be adjusted.

questionsToAsk: Based on my joint exam and blood work, how active is my RA right now, and what's the specific disease-activity target we're aiming for?
Am I a candidate for methotrexate first, and if it's not enough on its own, what would the next step — a biologic or a JAK inhibitor — look like for me?
What are the realistic risks and benefits of a JAK inhibitor for someone with my health history?
How often will I need bloodwork or imaging, and what results would tell us the treatment plan needs to change?
If I'm using steroids for a flare, what's the plan for tapering off them?
What symptoms should prompt me to call the office rather than wait for my next scheduled visit?

changelog.summary: Initial sourced content published: plain-language overview, research library, lifestyle guidance, and treatments.

disclaimer: This page provides general, plain-language educational information about rheumatoid arthritis and is not medical advice. Treatment options for RA continue to evolve, so always talk with a rheumatologist about how anything here applies to your own diagnosis and care.
